Senses.Explanation: To answer or act aptly at the juncture presented: respond as the occasion calls. A historical notice says Linji Yixuan frequently used shouts when responding, then immediately records his warning to followers who merely copied his shouting. Caoshan Benji is described as ordinarily responding with no fixed tracks; a lineage overview describes the five houses as each having a house style and responding in exchanges. The corpus also pairs the term with events and conditions: 'the teaching is originally without speech; it responds according to the affair,' and 'meet the occasion like lightning.' Zen bends ordinary situational responsiveness into an expectation of apt public answer and action. The occasion or juncture is what is presented; the word does not automatically mean a student's graded capacity or a generalized system.

meet the object and manifest a form
show a form in response to things
Zen responding to things, showing a form
Senses.Explanation: The phrase occurs 209 times in 105 allowlisted texts. The records repeatedly pair it with the comparison "like the moon in water" (如水中月). They also make it a public-interview question: asked "what is responding to things, showing a form?" Zhaozhou Congshen says, "bring the bed-seat over for me" (如何是應物現形；與我拈床子過來). In another exchange the monk asks which is the moon in the water comparison and the responding master raises the whisk. A later hall address says, "the body has no form; responding to things, it shows a form" (法身無象，應物現形), then raises the staff and measures the staff against the recorded heights of the World-Honored One and Maitreya. Thus the phrase is not left as an abstract proposition in the Chan corpus: masters put it into questions and answer it with the teaching-seat furniture and implements in front of the assembly.

Senses.Explanation: Answering the call records the audible response after one person summons another, preserving the call-and-response sequence of the case. To answer when called or to acknowledge an instruction. The word occurs 1,087 times in 227 allowlisted texts. Compilers repeatedly preserve the same audible action as the hinge of an encounter: Nanyang Huizhong calls his attendant three times and receives three answers; Shakyamuni calls Ananda after Ananda asks about the former buddhas' procedure; Mahakasyapa calls Ananda in the robe-transmission case; and Huangbo Xiyun names Pei Xiu by calling him, then declares the naming complete when Pei answers. In Xingsen's record an unnamed lecture master answers the call 'Lecturer,' and Xingsen immediately appraises him. Dahui Zonggao later raises an exchange in which Luoshan calls Zhaoqing and Zhaoqing answers before Luoshan replies 'a macaque enters the site of the Way' . The same response also acknowledges an instruction: Ananda answers Shakyamuni's order to enter the city with the bowl. The Zen bend is not a special second meaning but the records' placement of this ordinary answer as the next public turn and, at times, the central action of a named case.
